title: India bans battery waste exports to keep lithium and cobalt at home
subtitle: A DGFT order of 10 November stops the black powder from shredded batteries leaving India, so local recyclers get more to work with.
content_html:
Picture the battery inside an old phone that sits in a drawer at home. When batteries like that are crushed at a recycling plant, they turn into a dark powder. That powder is full of costly metals. Until this week, a trader in India was free to ship it to another country. On Tuesday, 10 November 2026, the government banned the export of this battery waste with immediate effect.

The order came from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT). The DGFT is the government office that writes the rules for what India can sell to, and buy from, other countries. The aim is simple: keep the powder in India, so Indian recyclers can pull out the metals and use them again.

What exactly did the government ban?

The new rule covers waste and scrap of cells and batteries that is unsorted and does not contain lead, cadmium or mercury. The notification names lithium-ion battery waste in this group. That is the type of battery found in phones, laptops and electric cars.

Every product that crosses India's border has an export policy. Some goods are "Free", which means anyone can ship them out. Some are "Prohibited", which means nobody can. The DGFT moved this battery waste to "Prohibited" until further orders; before this it was "Free". The order was made under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act of 1992 and the Foreign Trade Policy of 2023.

What is inside an old battery?

A lithium-ion battery stores power by moving tiny bits of lithium back and forth. These batteries were first sold in 1991, and they now power phones, laptops and electric cars. Three scientists who helped build them won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019.

When a battery dies, the useful metals do not vanish. Recyclers shred used batteries, or scrap left over from making new ones, and then take out the bigger bits of metal and plastic. What is left is a dark powder. Depending on the battery, it can hold lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite. The commerce ministry also lists manganese. These metals can be cleaned and used to make new batteries.

Think of it like a cricket bat with a cracked handle. The handle is broken, but the good willow in the blade can still be shaped into something new. The powder is the good willow.

Why does India want to keep the powder?

Lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese are called critical minerals. A country needs them to make electric vehicles, power storage and electronics, but India depends a lot on imports for several of them. Almost 90% of the world's capacity to process and refine these minerals sits in China, the same report says.

The ministry explained the thinking in a statement:

"Recycling battery waste is among the quickest and most sustainable ways of developing a domestic supply of these resources," the ministry said, as reported by The Economic Times.

The ministry also said India's capacity to recycle battery waste has grown a lot, but plants are not running full because they do not get enough raw material. Its hope is that the ban gives Indian recycling and refining units a steady supply, helps them use more of their machines, and brings in more investment and employment.

The Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), a trade think tank, says India can already process more of this powder than the country produces. So refiners are short of raw material. It is like a juice stall with three big machines but only one basket of oranges each morning.

Were big shipments leaving India?

Not on paper. GTRI said India recorded no exports under this product code in the year to March 2026. However, GTRI said the ban can stop future shipments and keep the powder for local refiners.

GTRI also pointed to a weak spot. The powder can carry toxic leftover chemicals and heavy metals, so shipping it already needs prior permission under waste rules. Some exporters, GTRI warned, may try to label the powder as cobalt powder or a nickel product to slip past checks. So customs officers will need to look at how a cargo was made, and not just at the label on the box.

This short video explains the ban and what the powder is.

Money for new metal plants

The ban came a week after a big spending decision. On 4 November 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a Rs 2,814 crore scheme to help build plants that process critical minerals in India. It runs over five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31.

Under the scheme, the government will pay 30% of the eligible cost of four plants. Two will process lithium, each with a capacity of at least 30,000 tonnes. Two will process nickel, each with at least 50,000 tonnes. Each lithium plant can get up to Rs 500 crore and each nickel plant up to Rs 900 crore. The scheme also plans for cobalt to be recovered as a by-product of nickel processing.

Put the two moves together. One keeps the raw powder inside India. The other helps pay for plants that turn raw material into pure metal compounds. It is like a samosa stall owner who first makes sure the potatoes stay in town, then gets help to buy a bigger kadhai.

Who gains and who has to change

  • Battery recyclers: Indian plants that turn the powder into metal should get more raw material to work with, the ministry said, so their machines can run closer to full.
  • Traders who shipped the powder abroad: under the new rule, they can no longer ship it abroad.
  • Battery and EV makers: more metal recovered at home could cut how much they import, GTRI said.
  • Young people looking for work: the ministry expects the move to bring more investment and employment into recycling and refining.

For now, the rule is clear. Battery waste of this kind stays in India.
